Batchly
Discovery → Prototype
Product discovery walkthrough

Batchly

The problem: dishes like casseroles, chili, and soup are nearly impossible to track accurately unless you divide them into precise, pre-weighed portions — this takes time, energy, and effort that keep people from adding home-cooked meals to their macro tracker.

Meet Sarah. Three kids, a slow cooker always going, a weight-loss goal she's serious about. Sunday she makes a pot of chicken and rice casserole — enough for the week. Her app (Lose It!) tracks recipes in servings, not by how much a serving weighs, so unless Sarah divides her casserole into pre-weighed servings to store in the fridge, she has no way to know what the macros are each time she serves herself a plate. By Wednesday she's guessing whether this bowl is one serving or one and a half. She's stopped trusting the number, so she's stopped logging the casserole at all.

Batchly fixes both ends of that: she weighs ingredients into the pot as she cooks, no re-taring or math — then weighs her bowl at dinner instead of guessing a serving count.

01 · Why This Problem Matters

Competitive landscape and market context

My core question going in to this research was: is there something out there that already solves the pain of tracking macros for home-cooked meals, or is this an open gap? I downloaded four competitor apps and did some market research that showed that the gap really does exist, and there is a market that would benefit from a solution.

Market context

  • The global diet and nutrition apps market is valued at roughly $5.8B (2025), projected to reach ~$10.2B by 2030 at a ~12% CAGR. [source]
  • An estimated 192 million people actively use nutrition/diet tracking apps worldwide. [source]
  • Retention is the industry's structural weak point: health and fitness apps broadly lose the majority of daily users within the first few days of install, and 30-day retention across the category averages in the single digits to low teens. [source]
  • AI-assisted photo and voice logging is visibly reshaping the category — most nutrition app roundups published in 2026 now lead with AI logging over manual entry [source] — a shift that trades accuracy for speed and underserves users who need precise macros.
Pulled from public web research under time pressure, not a single licensed report — sourced above rather than left as unlinked numbers.

Competitive landscape

ProductWhat it doesWhere it falls shortApprox. users (market share)
MyFitnessPal Manual per-ingredient recipe logging; recipes are saved against a declared serving count Heavy manual entry, plus a serving-count mismatch problem: once you declare "this makes 6 servings," accuracy depends on portioning leftovers to match that number, or remembering the per-serving gram weight days later ~280M+ registered users [source]
Lose It! Manual per-ingredient recipe logging; recipes are saved against a declared serving count Same serving-count mismatch problem as MyFitnessPal ~50M+ users [source]
Cronometer Recipe function records raw and cooked weight Still requires weighing each ingredient individually; no in-app place to record the cooking pot's weight — that has to be tracked elsewhere ~10M users [source]
MacroFactor Scoop a portion from a finished "combo" meal, record the weight Workflow is not user-friendly and makes the process of logging and tracking a recipe too complicated for the home cook. ~1.4M downloads [source]

None of the most popular apps on the market deliver the simplified, user-friendly workflow that home cooks need to be successful.

What this ruled in and out

The innovation here isn't new math — dividing raw macros by cooked weight already exists in spreadsheets and in Cronometer. What's missing is a friction-free workflow: cumulative weighing without re-taring between ingredients, in-app pot tracking, and one-tap portion logging. That reframed the product from "a better macro database" to "fewer steps to the same number."

02 · Primary Research

How the problem was found, and what people said

Starting broad

  • Surveyed mundane daily-life pain points people gripe about online — food/kitchen, public etiquette, tech/digital life, household — looking for friction that was common and underserved.
  • Food/kitchen surfaced a consistent cluster: people cooking mixed, one-pot meals find tracking macros for those dishes disproportionately painful, across Reddit, Facebook meal-prep groups, and fitness communities.
  • That narrowed the question to: "Why is tracking macros for one pot of chili so much harder than tracking individual ingredients, and what would it take to fix it?"

Qualitative research

  • Posted to Reddit and a Facebook meal-prep group asking about pain points — without mentioning any proposed solution, to avoid leading responses.
  • Ran two structured interviews.
  • Tested the four closest competitors firsthand: MyFitnessPal, Lose It!, Cronometer, and MacroFactor — details in Section 1.

What people said, and how it was weighed

Not a formal survey — the signal was built by counting independent, unprompted sources naming the same friction point. Six did, across two forums and two interviews: a directional pattern, not a statistically representative result.

Featured — Christine, mom of 2 who cooks one-pot meals on a weight-loss journey

A structured interview with a friend who matches the target user almost exactly. Her go-to dishes: chicken and rice casserole, chicken soup, stews, tuna noodle casserole. Asked one open-ended question — "What is the hardest part about tracking your food in your particular cooking context?" — she named two core pain points unprompted, without being led toward either:

  • She doesn't want to separate her leftovers into precisely-weighed portions.
  • She primarily cooks in one pot, weighing as she adds.

Asked how she'd want this to actually work, she said: "I'd love some kind of separate casserole calculator I could use while cooking and scooping out my portion, then I could just copy that right into Lose It! no problem" — describing the stand-alone companion model Batchly is built upon, unprompted.

SourceWhat they said or didSignal
Facebook meal-prep group (a mom, self-described "huge one pot person") Described the MyFitnessPal "create a meal, then figure out portions" flow as painful; wished for "a true lazy way that was also accurate" Pain point named directly and unprompted, by exactly the target profile
Reddit user, documented 65 lb weight loss Hand-built a Google Sheets system: per-ingredient density table, summed to a total, weighed after cooking, portions logged against density. ~5 min/day once set up. The exact workflow already exists as a manual workaround, plus proof the setup cost (not the ongoing use) is the real friction
Forum users, multiple threads Described a very complicated system that I personally did not even understand, involving logging fractional servings and lots of math. This problem is meaningful enough to users that they are willing to devise complicated workarounds

User interview — Marshall (MacroFactor user, 100+ lb weight loss) Eyeballs combo meals (e.g. chocolate cake) instead of tracking them, because MacroFactor is too clunky for multiple ingredients cooked together. Doesn't cook combo meals often enough for it to bother him personally. Even for someone who has lost 100 pounds doing this, MacroFactor's option for home-cooked meals is still too complicated.

Honest limits of this data

This is six sources, not five to seven structured interviews — the difference still matters. Forum posts are self-selected and can't be probed for follow-up the way an interview can, and two conversations is not five to seven.

  • Of the two interviews, Christine's closes the biggest gap in the rest of the data — she is the target persona, not adjacent to it the way Marshall is, and named both mechanics plus the companion-app model unprompted.
  • What this data supports well: the pain is real, named unprompted, by the right user profile.
  • What it doesn't yet support: precise frequency (how common is this, really?) or willingness to pay.
Standard practice for this kind of discovery is 5–7 structured interviews, asking "tell me about the last time you tried to do X" rather than "what would you do if" — people describe problems as solutions, and the real problem is underneath. Given a Monday-to-Thursday, four-day window, I substituted public-forum discovery (unprompted, unleading) plus two structured interviews for a full interview round. Section 4 outlines what a fuller round would add.
03 · Prototype / Proposed Solution

What was built

With Batchly, when Sarah wants to make a casserole, she puts the empty casserole dish on the scale and records the weight in the app. As she adds ingredients to the dish, she inputs the cumulative weight after each addition — no need to zero out the scale in between. When she's done, she taps "Ready to Cook," and is prompted to record the cooked weight once it comes out of the oven. When she's ready to eat, all she has to do is weigh her portion — and her macros are tracked for her home-cooked meal, just like they would be for anything else she logs.

Features

  • Cumulative weighing, no per-ingredient tare. The user enters the scale's current cumulative reading after adding each ingredient; the app tracks the running total in software, independent of the scale display.
  • Re-tare without data loss. If the physical scale gets re-zeroed mid-build, the app stores an offset and keeps computing the running total correctly — the actual fix for the friction point named in discovery.
  • Raw macros are conserved through cooking. Protein/carb/fat mass doesn't change when water evaporates, so cooked totals equal raw totals; dividing by cooked weight gives an accurate density per gram with no separate cooked-nutrition lookup.
  • Portion logging. Weigh a serving, get its macros via weight × density; the dish's remaining weight decrements automatically.

Scope

In scope (v1)
  • Quick and dirty HTML app to validate that the solution addresses the problem
  • Single-pot dish, cumulative weighing
  • Software-tracked running total & re-tare
  • Raw + cooked macro calculation
  • Portion logging with remaining-weight tracking
  • ~60-item curated ingredient library + custom entry
Out of scope (v1)
  • Multi-component plated meals (e.g. salmon + asparagus)
  • Volume-to-weight conversion (cups/tbsp)
  • Live nutrition database API / AI ingredient matching
  • Blended plate-average problem — documented limitation, not solved
  • Safari / iOS — v1 targets Chrome Desktop and Chrome Android only
Worth naming directly rather than leaving buried in scope docs: the target user is a mom on her phone in the kitchen, and a real share of that audience is on iPhone. Chrome-only in v1 means some of the exact people this is built for can't open it yet — an honest gap, not an oversight, and the first browser-support work I'd pick up next.

How it was built

Rather than building freeform, I used a structured, sequential method of using AI to build called Spec-Driven Development, in an agile-style workflow — each phase produces a written artifact before code gets touched.

User stories the prototype addresses

Epic 1 — Build a Dish

As a home cook adding ingredients to a pot, I want to enter the cumulative scale reading after each ingredient and see a running total of weight and macros, so that I can keep cooking without re-taring between every addition.

As a home cook whose pot is overflowing or who needs to switch pots, I want to re-tare the scale mid-build with one tap and keep cooking without losing any data, so that I'm never forced to stop tracking just because the scale needs re-zeroing.

Epic 2 — Log Portions from a Batch

As a home cook eating from a batch, I want to select a batch, weigh my portion, and instantly see its calories, protein, carbs, and fat, so that I can track what I'm eating without any manual math.

Built after Epic 1 by design — the density number this depends on had to be right first.

Epic 3 — Save & Reuse Dish Templates

As a home cook who just built a dish, I want it saved as a reusable template so I can find it again later, so that I don't have to re-enter the ingredient list every time I cook the same meal.

Rounds out the loop for repeat cooking — sequenced last since it builds on both epics above.

Full acceptance criteria for each story, plus the data model and scoping decisions behind them, are documented in the underlying project files and available on request.

Hypothetical — illustrative, not a real user quote

"Batchly is officially my Sunday routine now. I weigh the pot, toss ingredients in as I go, and by the time the casserole's in the oven I already know the macros. No more guessing what one bowl is worth on a Wednesday — I finally trust the number again."

04 · Retro

What went well, what didn't, what's next

What's still unvalidated

The prototype proves the mechanic works, and the signal from primary research is good for a four-day build — but signal isn't proof. Six sources and two interviews confirm the pain is real; they don't yet confirm:

  • How often this problem actually hits someone's week
  • Whether people would switch off their spreadsheet, or add a second app, to fix it
  • Whether Batchly's specific workflow — not just the idea of one — is what they'd actually adopt

That's the honest gap here, not a flaw in the build. The hypotheses below are what real validation looks like next.

Action items: hypotheses to test next

HypothesisHow to test it
Portion-logging (daily) sustains engagement even if new dish creation is only weeklyTrack ratio of portion-logs to new-dish-builds in usage data
In a free companion model, monetization comes from acquisition/revenue share, not direct paymentMeasure integration usage rates and correlation with retention in the partner app
Users want a focused companion tool that ports its data straight into their existing tracker, not a full standalone replacement for MFP/Lose It! — the end state is a one-tap push of a built dish's macros into whichever app they already log in. Already has direct, unprompted support from the target-persona interview in Section 2.Survey users at 30 and 90 days on standalone-vs-integration preference; track opt-in rate once one-tap push to a partner app ships
A mobile app is the right production form factor (v1 prototype is a webapp)Not yet tested — flagged as an open platform decision

Parked ideas, not yet validated

  • Shareable dish templates — "Mom's Turkey Chili, 247 cal/100g" as a reusable, shareable template; a possible content/acquisition channel.
  • "What's in the fridge" leftover tracking — surfacing remaining cooked weight as a daily-use inventory view, addressing retention.
  • Smart scale integration — Bluetooth pairing to remove the last manual step (reading and typing the weight).
  • Recipe import from the web — pull an ingredient list straight from a recipe URL instead of building it entry by entry, so setting up a template is closer to one paste than a manual build.

Expansion vision

  1. Companion integration — API connection to Lose It! or MyFitnessPal; push a built dish's nutrition entry to the primary tracker with one tap.
  2. Feature expansion — volume-to-weight helpers, multi-component plated meals, richer ingredient database via API or community contribution.
  3. Strategic outcome — if the companion model shows adoption, a natural acquisition target for an established tracker; if users signal demand for standalone use, expand into a full tracker built around the home-cook workflow.

What I'd do differently with more time

With more than four days: 5–7 structured interviews using "tell me about the last time you tried to track a mixed dish" rather than hypothetical framing, real theme-frequency counting instead of a five-source pattern match, and a check on willingness to pay before assuming the companion-app model is the right monetization path.
